{{Chess Opening Theory/Position|= |Trompowsky Attack| |rd|nd|bd|qd|kd|bd| |rd|= |pd|pd|pd|pd|pd|pd|pd|pd|= | | | | | |nd| | |= | | | | | | |bl| |= | | | |pl| | | | |= | | | | | | | | |= |pl|pl|pl| |pl|pl|pl|pl|= |rl|nl| |ql|kl|bl|nl|rl|= |moves=1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A45]] |parent=[[Chess/Indian Defence|Indian Defence]] }} =Trompowsky Attack= The [[wikipedia:Trompowsky_Attack|Trompowsky Attack]] is a new offbeat opening with less theory which involves White immediately putting the bishop on g5 attacking the knight. Usually in most variations (2...Ne4 or 2...e6) Black avoids doubled pawns, but sometimes accepts them (2...c5 or 2...d5). The latter of each pair (2...e6 or 2...d5) just mentioned can transpose into the Torre Attack after 3. Nf3; however the Trompowsky Main Line (2...Ne4) typically doesn't transpose after it's played.{{Wikipedia|Trompowsky Attack}}In the Trompowsky Main Line, both sides move their developed minor piece twice: Black's knight from g8 to f6 to e4 and White's Bishop from c1 to g5 to f4. Afterward Black has many options to develop unlike many other openings. Some possible developing moves include c5, d5, d6, or e6. A less common but also popular line involves 2...e6 (Classical Defense) when it is best '''not''' to trade pieces and instead develop naturally. This line can transpose into the Torre Attack with 3. Nf3 or continue with 3. e4 in the Trompowsky (Big Center Variation, which fits the position perfectly) and Black usually avoids the trade of minor pieces because of the pin (h6 and e5) and instead trades pieces directly with 4. Bxf6. Even less common but transposable is the move 2...d5 which asks for a transposition into the Torre Attack (3. Nf3) or the Richter-Veresov (3. Nc3) but White can take advantage of the move and stay in the Trompowsky with 3. Bxf6, doubling Black's pawns. Less common again is the 2...c5 line attacking the pawn. White can choose to push the pawn or trade pieces (3. d5 or 3. Bxf6). The former variation involves a "Poisoned Pawn Variation" which involves one side giving away a pawn for a opposing misplaced queen and a development lead. The variation goes 2...c5 3. d5 Qb6 4. Nc3 Qxb2. There is also the move 2...c6!?, which is less commonly played, but nonetheless quite sound. This could lead to similar positions as the 2... c5 line, related to the poisoned pawn variation, or this can lead to 1. d4 openings, such as the Richter-Veresov Attack or even the QGD/Slav Defenses. This line also contains a trap: white must be careful and avoid 3. e3??, where 3...Qa5+ loses the bishop on g5 to a fork. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} :'''1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5'''

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Indian defence |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A45]] |parent=[[../|Indian defence]] }} == 2. Nc3 == This is a less common move, with lots of transpositional possibilities. Developing the queen's knight this early is unusual in 1. d4 openings because it prevents White from playing c4. The knight supports playing e4 next. This usually forces Black to play [[/2...d5|'''2...d5''']], to prevent 3. e4. If White plays 3. e4?! anyway, the game transposes into a Blackmar-Diemer gambit position after 3...dxe4. However, the main ways for White to continue are 3. Bg5, the Richter-Veresov attack, or 3. Bf4, the Rapport-Jobava London system. An advantage of these systems is that they may be played against 1...Nf6 or 1...d4. Other moves allow White to play 3. e4 and transpose into a 1. e4 opening. '''2...e6''' 3. e4 d5 [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...Nf6|transposes into a French defence]]. '''2...g6''' 3. e4 d6 [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...g6|transposes into the Pirc defence]]. '''2...c5?!''' is a Benoni-style move, although the game plays out differently because of White's knight's position, preventing c4 but supporting e4. After 3. d5 e6, 4. e4 is now possible, and if Black continues to approach this [[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...c5/3. d5/3...e6|like a modern Benoni]], they may blunder 4...exd5?? 5. e5!4...exd5?? is the main move in the Lichess amateurs database; having been played over 350,000 times as of September 2026. (one line is 5...d4 6. exf6 dxc3? 7. Qe2+ Be7 8. fxe7 Qc7 9. bxc3 {{chess/not|+++}}). == Theory table == {{ChessTable}} {{Chess/theory table |line1=2...d5 3. Bg5 Nbd7 4. Nf3 h6 5. * [[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5|Closed game]] → [[../|Chigorin variation]] → '''2...Nf6''' * [[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6|Indian defence]] → [[../|2. Nc3]] → '''2...d5''' }} == 2...d5 == This position is commonly reached from either of move orders 1. d4 d5 2. Nc3 Nf6 or 1. d4 Nf6 2. Nc3 d5. Black now controls the e4 square with their knight and pawn. White's two main options from this position are both ways to develop their bishop. [[/3. Bf4|'''3. Bf4''']] is the '''Rapport-Jobava London system'''. From f4 the bishop pressures c7, and White has ideas around making an attack with Nb5. How Black deals with this threat steers the opening of the game. 3...e6 4. Nb5 Na6 with is one line, with the idea to later play ...c6 (kicking White's knight back) and ...Qb6 (to answer Bxa6 without doubling their pawns). Another approach is ...a6 (either immediately, 3...a6, or 3...c5 4. e3 cxd4 5. exd4 a6) which allows Black to develop their knight towards the centre of the board instead. [[/3. Bg5|'''3. Bg5''']] is the '''Richter-Veresov attack'''. If Black allows it, as after the traditional move 3...Bf5, White's usual idea is to trade bishop for knight and play against doubled pawns, 4. Bxf6 exf6, and they also have ideas of f3 and e4, Qd2 and O-O-O. The main move today is 3...Nd7: this removes the incentive to trade minor pieces because Black can recapture with the knight instead. 3...e6 defends the knight with the queen, but Black has to happy with transposing into a French defence after 4. e5. Black controls e4 twice and White once, so if White plays [[/3. e4|'''3. e4?!''']] anyway, it is a gambit of a pawn: the '''Hübsch gambit''', which may transpose to the Blackmar-Diemer gambit after 3...dxe4. [[/3. f3|'''3. f3?!''']] prepares to play 4. e4 and keep the pawn there. Black can counterattack White's loose d4-pawn with 3...c5 or 3...e6 4. e4 c5. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} :'''1.d4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5'''

== 3. Bg5!? · Richter-Veresov attack ==

White threatens Bxf6 (e.g. '''3...h6''' 4. Bxf6 dxf6). While this isn't a threat to win the d5-pawn, which is defended by the queen, White would be happy to reduce Black's control of the centre and play against Black's doubled f-pawns. Because White has prioritised developing their queen's side minor pieces, they also have plans to castle long and attack on the king's side. Another common theme is f3 to prepare e4. 

[[/3...Bf5|'''3...Bf5''']] is the old main line. It allows 4. Bxf6, the Veresov variation, where after 4...dxf6 Black's pawns are doubled. However, this is not a huge disadvantage and the game is equal. White usually continues with 5. e3 intending 6. Bd3 Bxd3 7. Qxd3 and trading off the bishops, so that they are only playing a knight against bishop rather than against the bishop pair. White's other approach is 4. f3, the Richter variation, where after 4...Nbd7 there are the lines 5. Nxd5, a temporary sacrifice intending 5...Nxd5 6. e4!, or 5. Qd2, intending O-O-O, Re1 and e4. 

Black has several options to avoid doubling their pawns.

[[/3...Nbd7|'''3...Nbd7''']] is the '''modern main line'''. Though for the moment this leaves Black's c8-bishop on the bench, it defends the knight with the other knight, and so disincentivises 4. Bxf6?! (4...Nxf6 and White has given up the bishop pair for nothing). Black usually looks to continue with ...d6 and ...Be7 to free their position. White's main options are 4. Nf3, the two knight's system, the immediate 4. Qd2 to prepare long castling and support playing e4, or 4. f3 to support e4. 

[[/3...e6|'''3...e6''']] defends the knight with the queen, though in so doing Black pins their own knight. Usually White plays 4. e4 and [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bg5|transposes into the classical French defence]]. 

[[/3...Ne4|'''3...Ne4?!''']] is the unusual '''Boyce defence'''. Black moves the knight with tempo on the bishop, but White gets to trade knights and is doing well after 4. Nxe4 dxe4 5. e3. 

=== History ===
An early appearance of this opening was in the Amsterdam 1889 tournament between Gunsberg and Burn.<ref>[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1661586 Gunsberg vs Burn, 1889. Chessgames.com]</ref> Amos Burn transposed to the line in the French that bears his name after 3...e6 4. e4 dxe4. 

This opening was explored in the mid-20th century by [[w:Kurt Richter|Kurt Richter]] and [[w:Gavriil Veresov|Gavriil Veresov]]. Richter preferred to play with 3...Bf5 4. f3, whereas Veresov favoured the continuations with 4. Bxf6. 

This is an offbeat, aggressive system. It is uncommon at the highest levels and even if White succeeds in doubling Black's pawns, Black is no less than equal.

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position|Indian Defence: Lazard Gambit}}

== 2...e5?! · Lazard Gambit ==
In a similar fashion to the [[Chess_Opening_Theory/1._d4/1...e5|'''Englund Gambit''']], Black sacrifices their e-pawn in the hopes of playing a trap after the pawn is taken, but is considered an unsound move in perfect play. Therefore, it is a rare occurrence in a real tournament game, but is not uncommon in amateur levels of play.

[[/3. dxe5|'''3. dxe5''']] accepts the gambit, and capitalizes on Black's dubious move, while gaining a tempo by attacking the knight on f6.

The main response is 3. d5, amassing space in the center similar to the Benoni. Black can continue down the Benoni with 3...e6; or, they can take advantage of White's c-pawn not being on c4 yet by playing 3...b5!, the Benko Defense (sometimes referred to as the Pseudo-Benko). 3. c4 transposes into an English Opening, Symmetrical Variation. Some 1. d4 players may try to play the Catalan setup with 3. g3?; this is considered a mistake due to 3...cxd4 4. Bg2 e5!, defending their extra pawn tactically; 5. Nxe5?? runs into 5...Qa5+ with a fork, winning the knight. Some 1. d4 players as White may try to stay consistent to the London with 3. c3 or 3. e3, which are the most common responses. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. :'''1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c5'''

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Queen's Pawn Opening |eco=[[Chess/ECOD|D03-D05]] }} == 2...d5 == The position has turned symmetrical again. White has many options to choose from, each one leading to very different opening systems. '''[[/3. c4/]]''' is the most popular, transposing into a Queen's Gambit. White may choose this move order to avoid certain openings, like the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e5|Budapest defence]], which would have been playable had White not placed their knight on f3 in advance. '''[[/3. Bf4/]]''' is the second-most popular, turning the game into a London System. '''[[/3. e3/]]''' sees White going for the Colle System. This is the main move-order used by practitioners of this system. '''[[/3. g3/]]''' turns the game into a Catalan-like position, but through a less accurate move-order. Black gets to place their light-squared bishop outside of the pawn-chain without any troubles. '''[[/3. Bg5/]]''' is the relatively rare Torre Attack. Unless White tries to double Black's pawns by exchanging the bishop for the f6 knight, this is an independent line. Otherwise it will likely transpose into typical Queen's Gambit declined lines. A move like 3. Nc3 is certainly not bad, but it doesn't put much pressure on Black. White's c-pawn plays a key role in control of the centre, and moving the knight to c3 earlier usually allows Black easy equality. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1. d4 Nf6 2. {{Chess Opening Theory/Position|= |Portuguese Opening| |rd|nd|bd|qd|kd|bd|nd|rd|= |pd|pd|pd|pd| |pd|pd|pd|= | | | | | | | | |= | |bl| | |pd| | | |= | | | | |pl| | | |= | | | | | | | | |= |pl|pl|pl|pl| |pl|pl|pl|= |rl|nl|bl|ql|kl| |nl|rl|= || }} =Portuguese Opening: 2. Bb5?!= The Portuguese Opening is a rare opening starting with the moves 1.e4 e5 2.Bb5?!. The bishop is ineffective on the b5 square when there is no black knight on c6. It can be easily attacked by Black's c-pawn with 2...c6. Other moves can result in a Ruy Lopez/Spanish Opening (like 2...Nc6 3.Nf3) or other situations, where Black should be fine. After 2...c6, the bishop can move to f1 (which makes White just waste 2 tempi), c4 (which allows 3...d5 to come with tempo and gives Black a classical center), d3, e2 (which allow a classical center for Black as well) and a4 (allowing 3...b5 4.Bb3 d5 and Black has a classical center, though engines may prefer 3...Nf6). On move 2, Black can also play Nf6, develop normally, and exploit the bishop on b5 later. The Portuguese Opening is akin to a Ruy Lopez where White does not play Nf3 and is trying to gain pressure on Black's d-pawn. White may be hoping that Black attacks the bishop too much and weakens their dark squares or overextends. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1.e4 e5 2.Bb5'''

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position|= |Bishop's Opening| |moves=1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C23]] |parent=[[../|Open game]] |responses=
*[[/2...Nf6|2...Nf6 · Berlin defence]] *[[/2...Bc5|2...Bc5 · Classical defence]]. }} == 2. Bc4 · Bishop's opening == With '''2. Bc4''' White develops their bishop to increase control over d5 and pressure f7, the weakest pawn in Black's position. The Bishop's opening is very transpositional: by not having played Nf3 yet, White retains the option of f4 and may plan to transpose into [[Chess/Vienna Gambit|Vienna]] or [[Chess/King's Gambit|King's gambit]] lines, or the game can be taken into a [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6|Russian]] or [[Chess/Italian Game|Italian]] direction. Compared to [[../2. Nf3|2. Nf3]], White has not threatened Black's e5 pawn, so Black is afforded flexibility in their reply. The main moves are 2...Nf6 or 2...Bc5. [[/2...Nf6|'''2...Nf6''']] and Black attacks White's e pawn. White may defend it or not. They can defend with 3. Nc3, transposing into a [[Chess/Vienna Game|Vienna game]], or 3. d3, happy that their king's bishop is already developed outside of the pawn chain. They can leave it undefended to develop 3. Nf3, transposing into a Russian game, or to counterattack with 3. d4 or 3. f4 (the Ponziani and Greco gambits, respectively). [[/2...Bc5|'''2...Bc5''']] is the classical response, developing Black's bishop. Transpositions to Vienna or Italian games are possible with 3. Nc3 or 3. Nf3. 3. b4 is a gambit resembling the [[Chess/Evans Gambit|Evan's gambit]]. The more original response is 3. c3, supporting an eventual d4 push. In amateur games, 3. Qh5 or 3. Qf3 may follow, expecting that Black will allow Qxf7#. Other second moves for Black include * [[/2...Nc6|'''2...Nc6''']], letting White whether to transpose into the Italian with 3. Nf3 or the Vienna with 3. Nc3, or hold off with 3. d3. * [[/2...f5|'''2...f5!?''']], the Calabrese countergambit, a sharp but not very sound gambit. * [[/2...b5|'''2...b5?!''']], the Anderssen attack, a Romantic but not very sound gambit. * [[/2...c6|'''2...c6''']], the Philidor counterattack, preparing d5, striking in the centre. * [[/2...d5|'''2...d5!?''']], the Khan gambit, to give up a pawn for the bishop pair (if 3. Bxd5 Nf6 4. Nc3 Nxd5 5. exd5) or two pawns for development (if 3. exd5 c6 4. dxc6 Nxc6), or a lead in development (if 3. exd5 Nf6 4. Nc3 Bd6) * 2...d6 to transpose to Philidor's Defence. === History === The Bishop's opening was popular in the 18th Century and a favourite of [[wikipedia:François-André Danican Philidor|Philidor]]. His 1790 book, ''Analysis of the Game of Chess'', largely focuses on this opening. In the 1930s, [[Wikipedia:Weaver Adams|Weaver Adams]] used to claim it was a "forced win" for White, but it's usually considered that Black can equalise with best play.{{Cite book |last=de Firmian |first=Nick |title=Modern Chess Openings |publisher=David McKay Company |year=1999 |isbn=0812930843}} Danish Grandmaster Bent Larsen revived the opening in the 1960s at the [https://www.365chess.com/tournaments/amsterdam_interzonal_1964/26079 1964 Amsterdam Interzonal]. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Berlin defence |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C24]] |parent=[[../|Bishop's opening]] }} == 2...Nf6 · Berlin defence == Black develops the king's knight and threatens the e4-pawn. This move also pre-empts "[[w:Scholar's Mate|scholar's mate]]" by controlling the h5 square so preventing 3. Qh5. === Defend the pawn === White's e4-pawn is under attack. Exactly how they choose to defend it presents different options for transpositions (Italian game positions or Vienna game positions). [[/3. d3|'''3. d3''']] is the '''main line'''. This is the most straight forward way to defend the pawn and puts paid to the idea of ...Nxe4. It also opens a line for the queen's bishop to develop. Most commonly, Black may invite White to transpose into an giuoco pianissimo via a couple of move orders (3...Nc6 4. Nf3 Bc5 is one). However, Black's most testing idea is to capitalise on the fact that they have not needed to play ...Nc6 yet by playing 3...c6, avoiding transposing and preparing to play ...d5. [[/3. Nc3|'''3. Nc3''']] is a transposition into the '''Stanley variation''' of the Vienna game. This appears to add a defender to e4, but the defence, for the moment, is illusory. If 3...Nxe4, 4. Nxe4? is a mistake on account of a common tactic called the centre fork trick. (4...d5! 5. Bd3 dxe4 6. Bxe4 f5 7. Bf3 {{chess/not|--}}). It's not cut and dry, however, because White can regain the material another way, 4. Qh5 (threatening Qxf7#) Nd6 (best) 5. Qxe5+ {{chess/not|=}}. Usually Black wishes to avoid this, and first defends e5, 3...Nc6, and if White wishes to avoid the centre fork trick, they are compelled to play 4. d3 to defend the pawn after all. This is a fine move, but it does allow Black to seize the bishop pair with 4...Na5. [[/3. f3|'''3. f3?''']] to defend the pawn should not be played: it is unnecessarily weakening to White's king's side, and takes away the most active developing square for the king's knight. === Gambit a pawn === White may rather give up a pawn for activity and attacking chances. After [[/3. d4|'''3. d4!?''']], the '''Ponziani''' or '''Urusov gambit''', White offers either pawn for Black to take. After 3...exd4, White allows Black the option of keeping the material: 4. Nf3 Nxe4 5. Qxd4 Nf6 {{chess/not|=}}. 4...Nc6 instead and the game reaches a tabiya more commonly seen in the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. d4/4...exd4|4...Nf6 line of the Scotch gambit]] (also arising from [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. d4|4. d4 in the Italian game two knights defence]]). Either way White has active play and compensation for the pawn. 3...Nxe4? however is wrong: 4. dxe5 and White is looking for sacrifices or attacks on f7, e.g. 4...Nc6 5. Bxf7+ Kxf7 6. Qd5+ Ke8 7. Qxe4 {{chess/not|++}}. [[/3. Nf3|'''3. Nf3''']] allows Black to take on e4, 3...Nxe4. Though 4. Nxe5 may be played, (Black is doing well after 4...d5), the usual idea is to sacrifice the pawn with 4. Nc3!?, the explosive '''Boden-Kieseritzky gambit'''. 4...Nxc3 5. dxc3 and White has a lot of activity. Many amateurs have fallen afoul of 4...d6?? 6. Ng5! Be6 7. Bxe6 fxe6 8. Qf3!{{chess/not|only}} {{chess/not|+++}}. However, Black can avoid all the complications with 3...Nc6, and instead transpose into two knights defence to the Italian game. [[/3. f4|'''3. f4''']] is a gambit explored by Gioachino '''Greco'''. Accepting the pawn, 3...exf4?!, would transpose into a less common line in the king's gambit accepted, but better refutations are to be had with 3...Nxe4 or 3...d5. === History === The earliest games in this line were recorded by seventeenth century chess author [[w:Gioachino Greco|Gioachino Greco]] (1600―1634), including the line with 3. f4, known as the Greco gambit.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1272151 NN v Greco, 1620. Chessgames.com][https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1272152 Greco v NN, 1620. Chessgames.com] [[w:Domenico Ponziani|Domenico Ponziani]] (1719―1796) published analysis of the defence, though focused more on the line with 2...Bc5.{{Cite book |title=The incomparable game of chess |last="dal Rio" |first="Ercole" |year=1820 |pages=228-232 |language=English |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=hvd.hn4zcu |translator-last=Bingham |translator-first=J. S. |orig-date=1769 |location=London |publisher=J. J. Stockdale}} (N.B. as a historical curiousity, the translator incorrectly attributed this to Del Rio rather than Ponziani) Before [[w:Carl Jaenisch|Jaenisch]], 2...Nf6 was considered inferior to 2...Bc5. Jaenisch praised 2...Nf6 as the strongest, counterattacking reply, writing in 1842 that it "proves... the relative weakness of [2. Bc4, and] It is difficult for us to conceive how all preceding authors have, without exception, dismissed [2...Nf6] as inferior to [2...Bc5], which latter move so decidedly yields a vast field of attack for the first player."{{Cite book |title=Jaenisch's chess preceptor: a new analysis of the openings of games |last=de Jaenisch |first=C. F. |publisher=Longman & co. |year=1847 |location=London |url=https://archive.org/details/jaenischs-chess-preceptor |translator-last=Walker |translator-first=George |pages=64-71}} (translation of {{Cite book |title=Analyse nouvelle des ouvertures du jeu des échecs |last=de Jaenisch |first=C. F. |publisher=Gartner |year=1842}}) It was given the name Berlin defence (in German, ''Berliner partie'') by [[w:Tassilo von Heydebrand und der Lasa|von der Lasa]] in ''Handbuch des Schachspiels'' (first published 1843), who attributed it to Berliner [[w:Ludwig Bledow|Ludwig Bledow]] (1795―1846).{{Cite book |title=Handbuch des Schachspiels |last=von Biluger |first=P. R. |publisher=Verlag Von Veit & Comp. |year=1891 |edition=7th |location=Leipzig |url=https://archive.org/details/handbuchdesscha00schagoog |pages=363-374}} ==Theory table== {{ChessTable}} '''1. e4 e5 2. ==Bishop's Opening: Walkerling==

===3. f3?!===

The Walkerling variation of the Bishop's Opening is a chess opening that begins with the moves 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nf6 3. f3!?. This move is considered an '''obvious error''' by chess experts, as it weakens White's pawn structure and hinders the development of the king's knight, as well as weakening the kingside.

Black's main options are:

:*[[/3...Bc5/]] develops the bishop to an active square that attacks f2.

:*[[/3...Nc6/]] aims to activate both knights to active squares and control the center.

:*[[/3...d5/]] strikes back in the center and fights for a lead in development, which black already has.
:However, Black cannot play 3...Nxe4?, aiming to win a rook with 4...Qh4+, because white simply has 5. Kf1!, simply being up a piece.

'''1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nf6 3. f3?!'''

=== 3...d5! ===

This move is an aggressive response to white's passive 3. f3!? as it strikes in the center and opens up more lines for black's pieces.

White's main options are:

:*[[/4. exd5/]] is the most popular and best option as it is an equal trade after 4...Nxd5 5. Bxd5 Qxd5.

:*[[/4. Bxd5/]] usually transposes to the 4. exd5 line, after 4...Nxd5 5. exd5 Qxd5.

:*[[/4. Bb3/]]?! is a dubious option as it does not accept an important pawn trade as 4...dxe4 5. fxe4 and white's kingside is very weak, but this might have something with because after 5. fxe4, white still has a pawn in the center and it opens up f3 for the king's knight.

:*[[/4. Bb5/|4. Bb5?!]] checks the black king, and its purpose is almost the same as 4. Bb3.

== 2...Qg5? ==
{{Chess/sideline}}
A suspicious move. Black threatens White's g2-pawn, thinking to take advantage of the fact that the early development of White's bishop left it undefended.

However, the pawn is poisonous. '''3. Nf3''' attacks the queen and forces it to move, and if 3...Qxg2? then 4. Rg1 Qh3{{Chess/not|only}} 5. Bxf7+!. It turns out Black's f7-pawn was hanging, because Black can't afford to take it back. 5...Kxf7?? Ng5+! wins the queen. 

Even if White does not spot the Bxf7+ tactic, many turn five moves are good for White because they are ahead in development and can easily gain time by attacking Black's queen and forcing it to move, e.g. 5. Nc3 Nf6 6. Rg3 Qh5 7. Rg5 Qh6 8. Rxe5+ Be7 {{chess/not|+++}} This illustrates the danger of developing one's queen early, unsupported by the minor pieces.

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Anderssen attack |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C23]] |parent=[[../|Bishop's opening]] }} == 2...b5?! == This ancient move from the romantic era was [[Wikipedia:Adolf Anderssen|Adolf Anderssen]]’s favourite. Black tries to emulate an [[Chess/Evans Gambit|Evan’s gambit in reverse]], but White can refute the risky gambit by acting early. White can snap up the pawn '''3. Bxb5''' and it's not transparent what Black is getting. Anderssen played both 3...f5 and 3...c6: After 3...f5, the '''Thorold gambit''', either 4. exf5 or 4. d4 seem pleasant for White. With the Bishop on b5, Black can't play Nc6 so there is no tempo gain if Qxd4, hence: * 4. exf5 Nf6 5. d4 exd4 6. Qxd4 and Nc6 isn't possible * 4. d4 exd4 5. Qxd4 and Nc6 still isn't possible. If Black meets 4. d4 with 4...fxe4?, then 5. Qh5+ g6 6. Qxe5+ and "Black can put the pieces back in the box."{{Cite book |title=The Bishop's Opening Explained |last=Lane |first=Gary |publisher=Batsford |year=2004 |isbn=07134 8917 0 |location=London |chapter=11. Bc4 g6''' is a deviation from standard opening principles in chess. The move '''2…g6?''' is considered weak because it allows White to seize control of the center with 3. d4 quickly. This move attacks the pawn on e5 and prepares to develop the knight to f3. After '''3. d4!,''' White plans to continue with 4. Nf3, aiming to put more pressure on the central square e5. Black cannot respond with 4... Bg7?? because 5. Nxe5 Bxe5 6. dxe5 would lead to White winning a pawn due to the pin on the e5 pawn. White could also consider a long-term plan of advancing the pawn on a2 to a5 (via a4) to control the b6 square. This move could potentially limit Black's queenside development and create weaknesses in Black's pawn structure. Overall, this sideline in the Bishop's Opening leads to a superior position for White due to Black's neglect of central control and weak pawn structure. == Theory table == {{ChessTable}}. == 3. f4?! · Omaha gambit ==

White attacks e5 with the flanking f-pawn, hoping to prise the pawn away from control of the d4 square and then build a big centre with pawns on both d4 and e4. However, White has weakened their king and will have to play around that danger.

White plays in the manner of the Vienna gambit, but this is an inferior version. In the Vienna gambit, after [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nf6/3. f4|2...Nf6 3. f4]], White can answer 3...exf4? with 4. e5!, kicking the knight back to g8, before defending their kingside with Nf3 and later recovering the pawn. White gets immediate compensation if the Vienna gambit is accepted, to the degree that 3...exf4? is considered a mistake.

However, in the Omaha gambit, there is no threat of e5, so '''3...exf4''' is critical. The resulting positions transpose into the Fischer defence to the king's gambit ([[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...exf4/3. Nf3/3...d6|1. e4 e5 2. f4 exf4 3. Nf3 d6]]), a line which includes ...d6 to prevent Ne5.

Alternatively, Black can ignore the gambit and allow White to take into them, '''3...Nc6''' 4. fxe5 dxe5{{Chess/not}}.

==Vienna Countergambit==
This is simply a King's Gambit reversed, but with Nc3 added for White. This makes it not sound - opening the kingside when you have less development is not a good idea. 
==Possible Moves==
3. exf5—After Nf6 to prevent Qh4+, there is g4! immediately gaining initiative. Not only are we a pawn up, but Black's kingside is also quite weak, while our kingside is quite safe. This leads to lines in the Kings Gambit where we are not only a tempo up, we have developed the queen's knight. This means we have more control over d5. Why divert the white e pawn to the f5 square when even if you build a center with d5-e5, it will be very shaky?

3. Nf3? - This directly transposes to the Latvian Gambit Declined, it is not the best, but white can still get a position with more development than black after 3...fxe4, 4. Nxe5 Nf6 5. Bc4, and Stockfish 16 gives this a +0,7 advantage. However there is no reason to decline the pawn.

3. d4 - This has a slight similarity to the Falkbeer Countergambit in the King's Gambit, since black can't take the e4 pawn because of Qh5+!, instead, black should play exd4 and white should play Qxd4, but there is also the astonishing, exf5, if black plays dxc3, white will play Qh5+ after Ke7, Bg5+ and Nf6, white can just play the absurd-looking move O-O-O if black were to take the pawn, Kb1!, sacrificing yet a pawn, and black has to deal with a lot of attacking possibilities, after d5, Nf3, white's a attack is really strong.

== 2...Bc5?! · Busch-Gass gambit ==

Black ignores the attack on their e-pawn to go on the offensive immediately. This gambit is considered unsound. 

After White accepts the gambit with [[/3. Nxe5|'''3. Nxe5''']], Black continues 3...Qh4 threatening mate. Black hopes to keep White on the back foot long enough to recover the pawn and get ahead in development. However, Black cannot get sufficient compensation so long as White keeps their head. 

Transposition into a [[Chess/Stafford Gambit|Stafford gambit]] is also possible, after 3...Nc6 4. Nxc6 dxc6.

A club-level continuation is declining the gambit with '''3. Bc4''', but this fails to capitalise on Black's play and gives them time to defend their e pawn with 3...Nc6 (transposing into a [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5|Giuoco Piano]]) or 3...d6.

== 3. Nxe5 ==
White captures Black's undefended e-pawn. 

Black's plan to justify the gambit is [[/3...Qh4|'''3...Qh4''']]. This threatens mate on f2 and looks to recover the e pawn. White can counter both threats with 4. Qe2, but the most critical line is actually 4. d4! Qxe4 5. Be3, giving up the pawn but achieving a crushing lead in development (5...Nf6 6. Nd2 Qf5 7. Bd3 Qe6 8. Nxf7 Qxf7 9. dxc5).

Black's alternative third move is [[/3...Nc6|'''3...Nc6''']], the Chiodini gambit, which transposes into a Stafford gambit after 4. Nxc6 dxc6. 

The wild sacrifice [[/3...Bxf2|'''3...Bxf2+?!''']] achieves nothing. [[/3...d6|'''3...d6''']] is probably the most sound continuation, but Black has to make peace with having given up a pawn in exchange for a slightly improved [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6|Philidor]].

== 3...Qh4 ==

'''3...Qh4''' threatens mate on f2 and looks to recover the e pawn. 

Black is perhaps hoping for '''4. g3??''', which prevents mate but allows 4...Qxe4 5. Qe2 Qxh1 -+, or '''4. Nf3??''', which blunders 4...Qxf2#. 

White can counter both the threat to f2 and e4 with '''4. Qe2!?'''. Black then hopes to develop faster and easier than White (White's queen is in the way of their bishop, for example) and that this will provide them with sufficient compensation for the lost pawn, but it is not borne out. A continuation might be 4...Nf6 (attacking e4) 5. Nc3 O-O 6. g3 Qh5 7. Qxh5 Nxh5 8. Bg2.

The most critical line is actually '''4. d4!''' Qxe4 5. Be3. White gives back the pawn but achieves a crushing lead in development instead (5...Nf6 6. Nd2 Qf5 7. Bd3 Qe6 8. Nxf7 Qxf7 9. dxc5).

= Mengarini's Opening =
=== 2. a3 ===
White plays a waiting move instead of developing a piece. This move is playable but timid and concedes White's first move advantage. This is similar to an Open Game with colors reversed, except that White has played a3 to stop Bb4 if Nc3 is played. Black can choose a variety of responses:

* 2...Nf6
* 2...Nc6
* 2...Bc5
* 2...d5
* 2...f5!?

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Centre pawn opening |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C20]] |parent=[[../|Open game]] }} == 2. c3?! · Centre pawn opening == White wishes to build a big, two-pawn centre, and plays 2. c3?! to support pushing the pawn to d4. This idea, c3 to support d4, is a common plan for White in many open games (games beginning [[../|1. e4 e5]]): c3 after developing the knight is the Ponziani ([[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. c3|2. Nf3 Nc6 3. c3]]), and it comes after developing the knight and bishop in the Italian and Spanish games ([[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. c3|3. Bc4 Bc5 4. c3]] or e.g. [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5/4. c3|3. Bb5 Bc5 4. c3]]3...Bc5 is a sideline today, the classical defence. The same idea occurs in the main line later: 3. Bb5 a6 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. O-O Be7 6. Re1 b5 7. Bb3 d6 8. c3, but the line is longer and makes for a worse illustration of the point.). However, played on White's second move without any pieces developed, it is simply too slow. Black can respond vigorously with '''2...d5''' to eliminate transpositional possibilities. After 3. exd5 Qxd5{{chess/not|-}}, there is no 4. Nc3 to chase the queen away and gain a tempo as the c3 pawn is occupying the square. Staunton suggested that by avoiding taking the pawn, White could keep the game competitive: 3. Nf3 dxe4 4. Nxe5 Bd6!? 5. Nc4 Be6 6. d4 exd3 e.p. 7. Bxd3{{chess/not|+}}. However, 4...Qe7! is an improvement, which forces White to move the knight again and gums up White's play for the centre, as d4 will be met with exd3 e.p. and a discovered check. Black sweeps ahead in development to a reach a dominating position. 5. Nc4 Nc6 6. Be2 Bf5 7. O-O O-O-O{{chess/not|-}}. === History === {{Chess/board |moves=1. e4 e5 2. c3 Nf6 3. Qc2 Bc5 4. Nf3 Nc6 5. Bb5 d6 6. d4 exd4 7. cxd4 Bb4+ 8. Nc3 Bd7 9. O-O |caption=Position given by Ruy López. |frame=1 |float=right}} 2. c3?! is very unusual today but has a long history. It is the first opening [[w:Ruy López de Segura|Ruy López de Segura]] chose to cover in his 1561 treatise, where he gives the line 2...Nf6 3. Qc2 Bc5 4. Nf3 Nc6 (López gives 4...Qe7 5. d4?? exd4 with threat of ...Qxe4 as an improvement for Black) 5. Bb5 d6 (a mistake, given it pins the knight) 6. d4 exd4 7. cxd4 Bb4+ 8. Nc3 Bd7 9. O-O{{chess/not|++}}.{{Cite book |title=The Art of the Game of Chess |last=López |first=Ruy |publisher=The Catholic University of America Press |year=2020 |location=Washington D.C. |pages=119-120 |orig-date=1561 |translator-last1=McGrath |translator-first1=Michael J.}} However, López reckoned without the reply 2...d5. By the time of [[w:François-André Danican Philidor|Philidor]] this was known to be the best retort, and on account of ...d5 he dismissed 2. c3?! as "very ill played."{{Cite book |title=Analysis of the game of chess |last=Philidor |first=F. A. D. |publisher=P. Elmsly |year=1790 |location=London |pages=50-63 |url=https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_analysis-of-the-game-of-_philidor-f-d-franco_1790_1}} After this discovery the opening must have fallen out of fashion. When [[w:Howard Staunton|Staunton]] analysed the opening in his 1847 book{{Cite book |title=The Chess-Player's Handbook |last=Staunton |first=Howard |publisher=Henry G. Bohn |year=1847 |location=London |pages=238-243 |url=https://archive.org/details/chessplayershan00staugoog}} (calling it the "'''the queen's bishop's pawn opening'''"), he offered a survey of previous analyses and surmised,
"This mode of commencing the battle was probably a favourite in the early days of European chess play, as Ruy Lopez has devoted more than ordinary space and attention to it in his often-quoted work of the sixteenth century."
Eric Schiller re-christened 2. c3 after '''MacLeod Call''', who "was not a very good player, but he was persistent in his use of this opening. At the 6th American Chess Congress of 1889, he relied on his pet opening, but finished at the bottom of the crosstable."{{Cite book |title=Unorthodox Chess Openings |last=Schiller |first=Eric |publisher=Cardoza Publishing |year=1998 |pages=239}} In recent years some databases have begun to call this, confusingly, the "'''Lopez opening'''". Unlikely to be in reference to Ruy López's book (from which 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 is the better known line, which more usually bears his name), the misunderstanding may have arisen from [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talk:Centre_Pawn_Opening&oldid=1101331183#Requested_move_22_July_2022 a longstanding editorial gaffe at Wikipedia]. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1. e4 e5 2. c3'''

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position|The Whale |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C20]] |parent=
* [[../|Open game]] * [[Chess Opening Theory/1. c4|English opening]] }} == 2. c4?! · The Whale == White controls d5 another time with a pawn instead of developing a piece. This move is playable but slow. It concedes White's first move advantage and has the drawbacks of creating a permanent hole on d4 and blocking the f1 bishop from developing to c4 or b5. Black has a wide range of reasonable options, including '''2...Bc5''', '''2...Nf6''', or '''2...Nc6'''. [[/2...g6|'''2...g6?!''']] is called the '''Adorjan defence'''. This prepares to fianchetto, though the king's bishop could already develop along the a3-f8 diagonal, and invites 3. d4! exd4 4. Qxd4 with tempo on the rook on h8. 4...Nf6 5. Bg5 where 5...Bg7?? loses a piece to 6. e5{{chess/not|+++}}. [[/2...c6|'''2...c6?!''']] transposes into the open variation of the accelerated Panov attack, though this improves White's position. Playing [[/2...d5|'''2...d5?''']] anyway is called the '''Bavarian gambit'''. === History === [[w:John Cochrane (chess player)|John Cochrane]] (1798―1878) experimented with this opening.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1271849 John Cochrane v Howard Staunton, 1842. Chessgames.com] The name, "The Whale", was coined by offbeat opening aficionado Eric Schiller, writing, "It seems to me rather large and lumbering... [https://ratings.fide.com/profile/2011204 Jennie Frenklakh] who lives close to whale territory in California played it in her early years".{{Cite book |title=Unorthodox Chess Openings |last=Schiller |first=Eric |publisher=Cardoza Publishing |year=1998 |isbn=0-940685-73-6 |location=New York |pages=143-144}} == References == {{Reflist}} === See also === {{Chess Opening Theory/Footer}}

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Leonardis variation |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C20]] |parent=[[../|Open game]] }} == 2. d3 · Leonardis variation == This insipid move is playable but concedes White's first move advantage. Inferior to most other responses to 1. e4 e5, 2. d3 defends e4, though it was not under attack. While it opens a line for the queen's side bishop to develop, it closes the line 1. e4 opened for the king's bishop. Should White wish to play d4 in the future, they have lost a tempo here. White misses the opportunity to develop a piece to make an unnecessary pawn move instead. Black is allowed easy equality with '''2...Nc6''' or '''2...Nf6''' followed by 3...d5. This can lead to a position like a [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6|Philidor defence]] with colours reversed: e.g. 2...Nf6 3. Nf3 Nc6 4. Be2 d5 5. Nbd2{{chess/not|-}} is the reversed Hanham variation. If White doesn't want to develop their king's bishop to e2 behind the pawn chain, their intention may to be to play in the manner of a King's Indian attack, where White builds a d3 and e4 pawn chain and the fianchettos the bishop to g2: though the move order [[Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...d5/2. g3|1. Nf3 (preventing e5) d5 2. g3]] is more accurate. There are also plans involving an early f4, a sort of inferior [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nf6/3. f4|Vienna gambit]], which are still equal but less popular. ==Theory table== {{ChessTable}} '''1. e4 e5 2. d3'''

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Centre game |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C21–C22]] |parent=[[../|Open Game]] }} == 2. d4 · Centre game == White plays '''2. d4''' to smash open the centre. White threatens to take on e5, but really they are provoking exd4, and planning to develop their pieces rapidly by opening up the d-file for their queen and bishop. White may yet gambit some pawns for even faster development. This is the explosive Centre game. Black has some options, but almost always takes the pawn. === Take the pawn === [[/2...exd4|'''2...exd4''']], the Centre game accepted, is Black's most common and objectively best move. This leads to several different sorts of game depending on how White would like to recapture. Recapturing immediately, 2. Qxd4, is most common. Sounder is to play 2. Nf3 first, intending to recapture the pawn with the knight, but the most aggressive continuation is is 2. c3, gambitting one or two pawns in exchange for getting a huge development lead. === Defend e5 === If Black doesn't take on d4, next turn White will be able to take Black's e5 pawn instead. So if Black doesn't want to accept the centre game, they have to find a way to defend e5: 2...d6?!, 2...f6?, or 2...Nc6. [[/2...d6|'''2...d6?!''']] defends with a pawn, but it is not ideal. White can take on e5 anyway, and after the d-pawn recaptures, trade queens and force Black to give up their castling rights: 3. dxe5 dxe5 4. Qxd8+ Kxd8. Alternatively. White can transpose into a Philidor defence with 3. Nf3. 2...d6?! is a transposition into the Maróczy defence, usually seen in the Pirc in the move order [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4|1. e4 d6 2. d4]] e5). '''2...f6?''' is much worse of course, as the f-pawn makes a lousy defender of the e-pawn. After 3. dxe5, Black dare not retake with the f pawn or face Qh5+! with their weakened kingside (see also the [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6|Damiano defence]]). The best way to defend is the most flexible, [[/2...Nc6|'''2...Nc6''']]. This transposes into a line in the Nimzowitsch defence called the Kennedy variation (usually seen via 1. e4 Nc6 2. d4 e5?!). If 3. dxe5, Black can retake 3...Nxe5, but may then be forced to move the knight again by 4. f4. Alternatively White can choose 3. d5, kicking the knight, which Black then reroutes to g6 via e7. If Black wishes to avoid accepting the Centre game then 2...Nc6 is probably their best alternative with the most practical chances. === Gambit e5 === If Black is having a fun time trading pawns in the centre of the board, or thinks that having a well-contested, even game might be too boring for them, Black may decide to just give up on e5 and counterattack instead. These moves are invariably bad. [[/2...d5|'''2...d5?''']] is the Beyer gambit. The idea is that if White takes the d5 pawn instead of the e5 pawn, Black can bring out their queen: 3. exd5? Qxd5 4. Nc3 (attacking queen) Qxd4 5. Qxd4 exd4{{Chess/not}}. Black gets an even endgame. Of course if White takes the e5 pawn as they had planned, this gambit is just bad. 3. dxe5 dxe4 4. Qxd8+ Kxd8 and White gets a favourable queen trade, forcing Black to lose castling rights. '''2...f5?''', sabotaging Black's own kingside, is simply losing whether White takes the e5 ''or'' the f5 pawn. === History === This opening had fallen out of favour by the early 20th century when it was thought White was unable to prove an advantage. It had some critical re-appraisal in the 1980s but remains a distant fifth sideline behind White's other second moves. == Theory table == '''1. e4 e5 2. d4''' {| class="wikitable" |- !   !! 2 !! 3 !! 4 !! 5 !! == 2...d6 ==
This is an inferior way to enter a Philidor. While White's best move is still Nf3, transposing into the Philidor, it gives the additional option of immediately entering an endgame with 3.dxe5 dxe5 4.Qxd8+ Kxd8 5.Bc4 (though engines have no trouble defending it for Black). Black would lose the right to castle, and White would have a lead in development. White can also enter a Chekhover-like position via 3.Nc3 exd4 4.Qxd4 with the intention to respond to Nc6 with a Bb5 pin, or alternatively drawing the queen back to d3 or e3 and simply enjoying a space advantage. As such, it is considered strictly inferior to the Philidor move order, because White's alternatives after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 are much less aggressive.

pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Centre game |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C21]] |parent=[[../|Centre game]] }} == 2...exd4 == Black takes White's d-pawn. === Retake the pawn === [[/3. Qxd4|'''3. Qxd4''']] is the main move. This allows Black to develop 3...Nc6 with tempo, forcing White to move their queen again. [[/3. Nf3|'''3. Nf3''']], the '''Kieseritzky variation''', allows White to prepare to retake the pawn with the knight instead. This avoids giving Black ...Nc6 with tempo. 3...Bb4+ or 3....Bc4 are playable, or there are several possible transpositions including 3...Nc6, transposing to the Scotch game, 3...d6 to the Philidor defence, and 3...Nf6 to the modern attack in the Russian game. === Gambit the pawn === [[/3. c3|'''3. c3''']] is the '''Danish gambit'''. White offers to let Black keep the pawn in return for rapid development. They may gambit one (3...dxc3 4. Nxc3) or two (3...dxc3 4. Bc4 cxb2 5. Bxc2) pawns in this way. This is playable, and White gets a lot of piece activity in compensation for the pawn(s). [[/3. Bc4|'''3. Bc4''']], the '''von der Lasa gambit''', is also playable. An independent line follows 3...Bb4+, but usually this transposes into one of several different gambits. If 3...Nf6, White can transpose into the Urusov gambit with 4. Nf6 (4. e5?! and Black is better after 4...d5!). After 3...Nc6 instead, White may yet play c3 and transpose into the Göring gambit (4. c3 dxc3 5. Nf3, with the idea 5...cxb2 6. Bxb2), or otherwise transpose into the Scotch (4. Nf3 Nf6, where the choice is 5. e5 or gambit the e-pawn as well with 5. O-O). [[/3. f4|'''3. f4?''']] is the '''Halasz-McDonnell gambit'''. Having deflected Black's pawn away from control of f4, White seizes space on the king's side. This gives Black time to defend their pawn, 3...Nc6, and they can gain initiative attacking e4, 4. Nf3 d5!, because White cannot defend it with Nc3 until they have removed Black's d4-pawn. Against best play White is not thought to have compensation for the pawn. [[/3. Bd3|'''3. Bd3''']] is the '''Ross gambit'''. This is a less ambitious square for the bishop. Black can defend the pawn with 4. Nc6 and White has partial compensation. ==Theory table== '''1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4''' {| class="wikitable" |- !   !! 3 !! 4 !! Evaluation !! Notes |- ! [[Chess/Center Game|Center Game]] | '''[[/3. {{Chess Opening Theory/Position|von der Lasa gambit |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C21]] |parent=[[../|Center game accepted]]}} == 3. Bc4 · von der Lasa gambit == White gambits their d4 pawn. After either 3...Nf6 or 3...Nc6, this will transpose into other openings. [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Bc4/3...Nf6|'''3...Nf6''']] is Black's most common move, transposing to the Urusov gambit which is more normally seen from the Bishop's opening with 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nf6 3. d4 exd4. [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Bc4/3...Nc6|'''3...Nc6''']] is another good move developing the queenside knight. This often transposes to the Scotch gambit after the normal and common developing move 4. Nf3. == Theory table == {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} {| ! !3 !4 ! |- !Urusov gambit

pages.title: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Nf3
pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position|Kieseritzky variation |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C21]] |parent=[[../|Center game accepted]]}} == 3. Nf3 · Kieseritzky variation == White brings another attacker to Black's d4 pawn. This often transposes to other openings, though independent lines exist. [[/3...Nc6|'''3...Nc6''']] is the most common move, transposing to the Scotch game, more normally seen from the move order 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4. [[/3...Bc5|'''3...Bc5''']] is another normal move, developing the bishop. This can go two ways; 4. Nxd4 Nc6 transposes into the Classical Scotch game, while 4. c3 is the Lanc-Arnold gambit, an independent option. === History === [[w:Lionel Kieseritzky|Lionel Kieseritzky]] (1806-1853) was a German chess master. Kiesertizky played this line in a blind simul in 1851, and annotated and published the game in ''La Régence'', the chess journal he edited.{{Cite journal |title=Parties entre les plus forts joueurs de l'epoque |journal=La Régence; journal des échecs |url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_UBRBAAAAYAAJ |volume= |issue=5 |pages=137-154 |year=1851}} (Game is No. CLXXI pp 149-150)[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=2798196 Kieseritzky v Witcomb, 1851. Chessgames.com] == Sample game == '''Lionel Kieseritzky vs Henry Witcomb'''
'''21 April 1851. Blind simul.''' {{Chess/board|moves=1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. Nf3 c5 4. Bc4 d6 5. Ng5 Nh6 6. c3 Nc6 7. f4 Na5 8. Bd5 Bg4 9. Qa4+ Bd7 10. Qc2 dxc3 11. Nxc3 f6 12. O-O|caption=In this position, Black plays 12...fxg5? and loses.|frame=1|float=right}} '''1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. Nf3''' White prepares to recapture the pawn with the knight instead of the queen. This gives Black the opportunity to defend and hold on to the pawn. '''3...c5 4. Bc4 d6 5. Ng5 Nh6''' White makes an attack on the f7 square with knight and bishop; Black defends. '''6. c3 Nc6 7. f4''' "A necessary move to prevent the Knight from moving to d5," Kieseritzky explains (translated). '''7...Na5 8. Bd5 Bg4 9. Qa4+ Bd7 10. Qc2 dxc3 11. Nxc3 f6??''' A mistake to give up control of the e6 square. In addition, the pawn is not really threatening to take the knight yet (see game continuation). '''12. O-O''' This sets a trap by allowing Black to take the knight. An alternative is 12. Ne6, attacking the queen. 12...Bxe6 13. Bxe6 and the bishop dominates Black's king and is difficult to dislodge (13...Qe7 14. Nd5! prevents ...Qxe6 due to Nc7+ winning the queen. 13...Nc6 intending ...Nd4 is stymied by 14. Be3.) 12...Qc8 13. f5 secures the outpost for white. '''13...fxg5? 13. fxg5''' Black now must move or lose the defender of the f7 square. Black could have limped on if they had instead given room to their king: 13...Qe7 14. Nf3 {{chess/not|+++}}. '''13...Ng4?? 14. Bf7+ Ke7 15. Nd5#''' "Capital error," writes Kieseritzky of 13...Ng4??. He advises Black should have given up the piece with 13...Qb6 14. gxh6 O-O-O to allow the game to continue and "conditions would be equal for both sides." Kieseritzky underestimates his position: material may be equal but White is completely dominant. == Theory table == {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} {{Chess/theory table |line1=3...Nc6 4. Nxd4 Nf6 |name1=Scotch game, Schmidt variation
(by transposition) |line2=3...Bc5 4. Nxd4 Nc6 |name2=Scotch game, Classical variation
(by transposition) |line3=3. ... ... 4. c3 |name3=Lanc-Arnold gambit }} {{ChessMid}} == References == {{reflist}} === See also === {{Chess Opening Theory/Footer}} {{BookCat}}

At the time, all four central squares are controlled by White. This may seem like a huge advantage for White, but if Black simply plays Nc6, the queen is forced to move. Conversely, it may seem like a bad idea to develop the queen before any other pieces; however, Black can get into trouble if careless. === Black's responses === Usually, Black responds to the center game by playing '''[[/3...Nc6/]]''' forcing White's queen to leave its central outpost. ==Theory table== '''1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. By far, the most popular move is '''4. Qe3''' – Paulsen's Attack – lining up the queen with Black's king. Most of White's other possible queen retreats allow Black a quick d5 to at least equalize - though most disastrous would be '''4. Qc3''', allowing 4...Bb4 to win the queen with a pin. The move '''4. Qd1''' allows d5 a few moves later in an even worse scenario than usual for White. Black then usually responds with 4...Nf6, deciding to focus on developing the other knight. On occasion, White chooses '''4. Qa4''' (mimicking the Scandinavian Main Line) or '''4. Qc4''' (the Hall Variation). == Theory table == '''1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. {{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Danish Gambit |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C21]] |parent=[[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4|Centre game]] → |responses=
* [[/3...dxc3|3...dxc3 · Danish Gambit Accepted]] * [[/3...d5|3...d5 · Sörensen Defence]] * [[/3...Ne7|3...Ne7 · Svenonius Defence]] }} == 3. c3 · Danish gambit == This is an aggressive gambit which, if accepted, leads to a tactical game. Before retaking the pawn, White allows Black to take a second one first. White hopes to use the tempi to get their pieces developed, while Black busy capturing pawns. After [[/3...dxc3|'''3...dxc3''']], '''accepting''' the gambit, White has two choices. After 4. Nxc3, Black is up a pawn, but in exchange White has a piece developed and is the only one with a pawn in the centre. More common is 4. Bc4, giving Black the chance to win another pawn: 4...cxb2 5. Bxb2, White is down two pawns but in compensation has two pieces developed and centre control. While engines find that Black has a slightly edge in the Danish gambit accepted, the lines are nevertheless dangerous to face because of White's piece activity. Therefore it is more common for Black to '''decline''' the gambit at this stage, with [[/3...d5|'''3...d5''']], the '''Sörensen defence'''. In lieu of giving White piece activity, Black allows White to recover the pawn, 4. exd5 Qxd5 5. cxd4, [[/3...Qe7|'''3...Qe7''']] is an uncommon but sound sideline, where Black stays up one pawn without giving White so much of a development lead. This covers the main moves. Black has a few other moves to give back the pawn, but these are atypical: [[/3...Nc6|'''3...Nc6''']] is the most common way to decline the gambit at the amateur level. 4. Nf3 transposes to the Göring gambit more commonly seen in the Scotch game move order, which may still be declined with ...d5. Otherwise, 4. cxd4 d5 5. e5, White regains the material and has more space. [[/3...d3|'''3...d3!?''']] to decline the gambit is inferior, as it allows 4. Bxd3, where White both recovers the material and develops a piece. [[/3...Ne7|'''3...Ne7''']] is called the '''Svenonius defence'''. === History === The gambit is named for [[w:Martin Severin From|Martin Severin From]] (1828―1895), a Danish chess master who played it extensively including at a major tournament in Paris in 1867.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chess.pl?tid=79227 Paris (1867). Nf3 - Rhubarb Gambit]] }} =Danish Gambit Accepted= The Danish Gambit Accepted is popular among club players, but not so popular at the highest level. That is because, it is easy for black to fall into one of the many traps on this line, but if black knows what to do, white can get no more than equality out of the opening. White has two main options from this position: :[[/4. Bc4/|'''4. Bc4''']] - Double Danish Gambit :[[/4. Nxc3/|'''4. Nxc3''']] - Single Danish Gambit Although it may have been known earlier, Danish player Severin From essayed the gambit in an 1867 Paris tournament and he is usually given credit for the opening. The Danish gambit was popular with masters of the attack including Alexander Alekhine, Frank Marshall, Joseph Henry Blackburne, and Jacques Mieses, but as Black's defenses improved it lost favor in the 1920s. Today it is rarely played in top-level chess. White will sacrifice one or two pawns for the sake of rapid development and attack. With care, Black can accept one or both pawns safely, or simply decline the gambit altogether. ==Theory table== '''1. e4 e5 2. d4 exd4 3. c3 dxc3'''

== 4.Nxc3 ==
This move was Alekhine's choice. This move regains the one of the lost pawns, thus keeping White's material deficit to a minimum. White now has a huge lead in development and a central pawn.

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |King's knight gambit |eco=[[Chess/ECOC|C33]] |parent=[[../|King's gambit accepted]] |responses=
* [[/3...g5|3...g5 - Classical variation]] * [[/3...d6|3...d6 - Fischer defence]] * [[/3...d5|3...d5 - Modern defence]]}} == 3. Nf3 == '''3. Nf3''' develops a knight and controls the h4 square. This is important to prevent Black from playing Qh4+, exploiting the diagonal White opened with 2. f4. White now threatens to play d4 and recover the pawn they gambitted with Bxf4. Black would like to hold onto the f4 pawn if possible. There is a huge variety of approaches, but the most common replies are [[/3...g5|'''3...g5''']], [[/3...d6|'''3...d6''']], and [[/3...d5|'''3...d5''']]: the classical, Fischer, and Modern defences. === Defend the pawn === The best way to defend the f pawn is with another pawn, and the only one available is the g pawn. Defending the f4 pawn with a piece is not ideal: 3...Bd6? blocks in Black's d pawn and can be kicked around by e5, likewise 3...Qf6? 4. e5 and the queen can't stay defending the f pawn (4...Qf5? 5. d4 d5 6. Bd3). [[/3...g5|'''3...g5''']] immediately is the '''classical variation''' and main line. As well as protecting the f4-pawn, it threatens to advance to g4 and kick the knight away from f3. Black is not worried about weakening their own kingside because the f4-pawn gives Black all the space on that wing. Any kingside advance from White will run into Black's kingside advance coming the other way. The most common continuation after 3...g5 is for White to undermine the pawn chain with 4. h4. Then 4...g4 kicks the knight to 5. Ne5, the Kieseritzky gambit. 4...h5 does not work for Black as after White plays hxg4, the h5 pawn is pinned to Black's rook. The next most common is 4. Bc4, which most often leads to the Muzio gambit. Since f4 is not actually under threat until White has played d4, Black can delay ...g5 and first play a preparatory move, ...h6 or ...d6: [[/3...h6|'''3...h6''']] is the '''Becker defence'''. This prepares 4. d4 g5 5. h4 Bg7. Black's bishop defends their rook, allowing Black to meet 6. hxg5 with ...hxg5. [[/3...d6|'''3...d6''']], the '''Fischer defence''', is the move by which Bobby Fischer claimed to have refuted the entire king's gambit.{{cite web | url=http://brooklyn64.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/a-bust-to-the-kings-gambit.pdf | author=Fischer, Bobby | title=A Bust to the King's Gambit | year=1961 | accessdate=2020-05-21 | publisher=brooklyn64.com | archive-date=2025-05-26 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201111193505/http://brooklyn64.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/11/a-bust-to-the-kings-gambit.pdf | url-status=dead }} Black would still like to play 4...g5 next move, but first takes the precaution of denying the f3-knight access to e5. This means that after 4. d4 g5 5. h4 g4, 6. Ne5 isn't possible and the knight may have to make an abject retreat to g1. In this way, 3...d6 avoids the Kieseritzky gambit, although as the Kieseritzky gambit actually doesn't score very well for White, Black is usually happy to allow it and play the 3...g5 variations instead. === Keep initiative: attack the centre === Black knows that f4 isn't under threat immediately: White has to move their d-pawn first. If Black keeps making threats, they can keep the initiative and disallow 4. d4 or 4. d3 by tempo. Thereby, they prevent the discovered attack on f4 and defend it that way. The first approach to keep the initiative is to attack the centre, with either ...d5 or ...Nf6. [[/3...d5|'''3...d5''']] is the '''modern defence'''. 3...d5 attacks the e4 pawn, so White doesn't have the opportunity to move the d pawn and pick up the f pawn (for example, 4. d3? dxe4 5. dxe4 Qxd1+ 6. Kxd1 Bd6 {{Chess/not|-}}). After 4, exd5, ''now'' White can defend the f pawn with 4...Bd6, as in this position Black's d pawn has already moves, and there is no threat of e5 to kick the bishop, or attack the d5 pawn with 4...Nf6. However, this defence is one of the few King's Gambit lines that score better for White than Black. A variation on the modern defence is to prepare ...d5 with [[/3...Ne7|'''3...Ne7''']], the '''Bonsch-Osmolovsky variation'''. Then if White trades on d5, Black can get a knight there to defend f4: 3...Ne7 4. d4 d5 5. exd5? Nxd5. However, exd5 isn't forced: White can meet 4...d5 with Nc3 to defend the pawn instead. [[/3...Nf6|'''3...Nf6''']] is the '''Schallopp defence'''. The knight attacks the e4 pawn. After 4. e5 the knight routes to ...Nh5!, protecting the f pawn. After 5. d4 Black can chip away at the centre with ...d6. A example continuation: 6. Qe2 dxe5 7. Nxe5 Qh4+ 8. g3 Nxg3 9. hxg3 Qxh1 10. Bxf4 {{Chess/not|--}}. That Black can spend two moves putting a knight on the edge of the board and still win 35% of games (vs 31% for White) is probably a bad omen for King's gambit players. Alternatively White can respond 4. d3 to defend the e4 pawn. Black has to allow Bxf4 (4...g6? 5. Nxg6 now works, as Black's knight is in the way of 5...Qxg4) to recover the pawn. 4...d5 5. Bxf4 dxe4 6. Qe2 Bd6 7. Bxd6 Qxd6 8. Nbd2 O-O 9. dxe4 Re8 {{Chess/not|unclear}}. An interesting try for White is 4. Nc3: protecting e4 and preparing to add an extra attacker on to f4 (4...Nh5? 5. d4 d6 6. Nd5 {{Chess/not|+}}). === Keep initiative: attack the kingside === The second way to keep the initiative is to renew the threat to White's kingside. [[/3...Be7|'''3...Be7''']] is the '''Cunningham defence'''. Forming a battery between the queen and bishop, it renews Black's the threat of a check on h4. Now if 4. d4?! Bh4+ 5. Kd2 (5. Nxh4? Qxh4+! 6. Kd2) White's king has been forced to move and will be stuck in the centre for some time. White's correct rebuttal is 4. Bc4. This means 4...Bh4+ can met with 5. Kf1. The usual response to 4. Bc4 is 4...Nf6, but then what's the point of having the bishop on that diagonal? === Minor lines === Minor lines include: * [[/3...f5|'''3...f5''']], the '''Gianutio countergambit'''. Black thinks White is having a lot of fun giving away their pawns, so offers their own f pawn to deflect White's e pawn. After 4. exf5 d5, Black looks to recover the pawn with Bxf5. * [[/3...h5|'''3...h5''']], the '''Wagenbach defence'''. Black wants to start storming White's kingside with pawns straight away. * [[/3...Nc6|'''3...Nc6''']], the '''Macleod defence''', is usually followed by 4. d4 d5 to prevent White's pawn coming to d5, 5. exd5 Qxd5 6. Nc3 Bb4. == Theory table == {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} 1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3. Nf3

Here White doesn't have a promising way to stop the check on h4, as 4.g3?! fxg3 5.hxg3 Nf6 saddles White with a weak isolated pawn on g3, and the semi-open h-file cannot be effectively used. If he tries h4?! Nf6, he creates all sorts of weaknesses down the g-file, and further delays his development. He has two main continuations: 4.Bc4 and 4.Nc3, while d4!?, gaining central space, freeing d2 for the king, and preparing to round up f4 with Bxf4, may be playable as well. 4.Bc4 is the main line, clearing f1 for the White king to move to and eyeing a possible attack on f7. 4.Nc3, however, is also good, with simple development. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. 1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 Be7

pages.title: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...exf4/3. Nf3/3...d6/4. d4
pages.wikitext:
d4 grabs the d4-e4 classical center and opens up the c1 bishop's attack on the f4 pawn. 

Black usually responds with g5, temporarily defending the pawn while planning ...g4 to attack the f3 knight and expose White to Qh4+.

The piece sacrifice line: Nc3 g4!? Bxf4 gxf3 Qxf3 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 O-O-O Qh4 Kb1! (get out of the way of diagonal) O-O-O. This is unclear.

Some play h4 to attack the g5 pawn and prevent Qh4+. This is around equal with best play.{{BookCat}}

[[/4. h4|4. h4 - Main Line (Paris Attack)]]
[[/4. Bc4|4. Bc4 - Classical Variation]]
[[/4. d4|4. d4 - Rosentreter Gambit]]
[[/4. Nc3|4. Nc3 - Quaade Gambit]]|=}}Black has put a pawn on g5 to defend f4. Left to their own devices, Black could reinforce this pawn with ...h6 and ...Bg7 and turn the f4-pawn into a fortress. However, the most common and forcing threat is for Black to play ...g4, flush White's knight away, and play Qh4+ to force White's king to go uncastled. White has two direct defenses and two indirect defenses to defend against ...g4. * [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...exf4/3. Nf3/3...g5/4. h4|'''4. h4''']]! is the most mainline direct defense against ...g4, as now the Black queen cannot make use of h4 with check. This move catches Black off guard, because g5 is attacked twice and defended only once, and 4...h6? doesn't protect it (5.hxg5 hxg5?? 6.Rxh8 is a disaster). 4...gxh4 would leave Black with three isolated pawns on the kingside. So the pawn advances to g4 and kicks the knight. * [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...exf4/3. Nf3/3...g5/4. Bc4|'''4. Bc4''']] is the most commonly-played direct defense against ...g4, vacating the f1 square for the White king to hide after Qh4+. Black could reinforce their g-pawn with ...Bg7 and ...h6, but much more common is ...g4, leading to some of the most famous variations such as the '''Muzio Gambit''', '''Lolli Gambit''', and '''Salvio Gambit'''. White can either sacrifice their knight and develop, sacrifice the bishop on f7 to lure out Black's king, or play Ne5 and coordinate on f7. * [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...exf4/3. Nf3/3...g5/4. d4|'''4. d4''']] is an indirect defense against ...g4, opening up the dark-squared bishop to recapture on f4. After ...g4, White can either play Nc3 or Bxf4 and give up the knight for an attack, or play Ne5, allowing ...Qh4+, but after g3 fxg3, Qxg4 saves the day. If Black goes for the rook with g2+, the position is equal! In fact, White gets an attack so extreme that it's very easy for Black to blunder the game away. * [[Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...exf4/3. Nf3/3...g5/4. Nc3|'''4. Nc3''']] is an indirect defense against ...g4, seemingly ignoring the threat on ...g4 but presenting a very strong counterattacking idea; after Ne5 Qh4+ g3 fxg3 Qxg4 g2+ Qxh4 gxh1=Q, White can go for a Scholar's Mate, and one day, the knight on c3 will jump to d5 with devastating effect. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. From here, Black has two main options; continue with 4...Bg7 development, or push forward with their plans with 4...g4 to unseat the f3 knight. After the latter, there are many great aggressive options for White. * The most popular continuation is the '''Muzio Gambit''' with 5.O-O, giving up the f3 knight but establishing a monstrous lead in development, with which White will mercilessly attack Black. * Another fun option is the '''Lolli Gambit''' with 5.Bxf7+, sacrificing the bishop on f7 but luring Black's king out into the open, giving rise to another ripe attacking position for White. * A more mainline option is the simple 5.Ne5, the '''Salvio Gambit'''; after 5...Qh4+, we see the deeper point behind the earlier 4.Bc4; White can now play Kf1 (similar to the King's Bishop Gambit). White pursues an attack against Black, down only a pawn instead of a piece. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. 1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4

pages.wikitext:
= King's Gambit Accepted, Rosentreter Gambit =
With 4.d4, the '''Rosentreter Gambit''', White ''indirectly'' defends against Black's threat of 4...g4. The most basic point is that White opens up their dark-squared bishop to recapture the f4 pawn. Most common by far is 4...g4 indeed, after which White has three very deadly options.

The most played and trickiest option is 5.Ne5, and after the ensuing 5...Qh4+ 6.g3 fxg3, 7.Qxg4 saves the day for White. The point is that Black's tempting move 7...g2+ is not best; after 8.Qxh4 gxh1=Q, Black has won White's rook, but after 9.Nc3, Black's position is extremely delicate; the engine evaluates this as equal, and it's extremely easy for Black to blunder. This line demonstrates very well how 4.d4 indirectly defends against 4...g4.

Another option is to play 5.Bxf4, the '''Testa Gambit'''; White sacrifices their f3 knight in similar fashion to the Muzio Gambit, looking for a deadly attack.

The third option is 5.Nc3, the '''Sorensen Gambit'''; once again, similar to the Testa and Muzio Gambits in sacrificing the f3 knight, but trying to demonstrate counterplay with the c3 knight instead of the dark-squared bishop.

Nf3/3...g5/4. h4/4...g4|'''4...g4''']]. * 4...f6? simply loses the pawn to 5.Nxg5! since 5...fxg5 6.Qh5+ Ke7 7.Qxg5+ Nf6 8.e5 leads to a winning advantage for White. * 4...h6?! also loses the pawn, as 5.hxg5 hxg5 permits 6.Rxh8. Black has no better option but to allow 5...Bg7 6.gxh6 Rxh6 7.Rxh6 Bxh6. This gives White the advantage. * 4...gxh4? leaves Black with a terrible pawn structure - doubled isolated pawns on f4, h4, f7, and h7. White doesn't have to capture them right away, often instead playing 5.d4. * 4...Bh6 or 4...Be7 followed by 5.hxg5 Bxg5 6.d4! allows White to win the f-pawn back with the move g3 while remaining ahead in development. Black does have one accurate alternative move to 4...g4, which is to counterattack in the center with 4...d5!? The line often continues with 5. d4! dxe4 Nxg5 Nf6 which is unclear. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. 1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4. h4

pages.title: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...c5/3. d5
pages.wikitext:
{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Benoni defence |parent=[[../|Benoni defence]] |responses=
* [[/3...b5|3...b5 · Benko gambit]] * [[/3...e6|3...e6 · Modern Benoni]] * [[/3...e5|3...e5?! · Czech Benoni]] * [[/3...d6|3...d6 · Hromádka system]] * [[/3...Ne4|3...Ne4?! · Vulture defence]] }} == 3. d5 == White keeps their central pawn and takes more space in the centre. White's pawn dug in on d5 cramps Black's position. How Black will crack the pawn chain, now or later, determines the direction of the game. === Attack the pawn chain immediately === [[/3...e6|'''3...e6''']], the '''Modern Benoni''', attacks the tip of the pawn chain. After the trades 4. Nc3 exd4 5. cxd4 d6 6. e4, Black surrenders space to White and has a weak pawn on d6, but in return gets excellent play on central dark squares, a queenside majority, and use of e5. Black's main ideas are to play on the queenside, while White targets the weak d6 and attacks on the kingside. [[/3...b5|'''3...b5''']], the '''Benko''' or '''Volga gambit''', targets the base of the pawn chain. Black's idea is long term positional pressure: they offer a pawn in the hope of opening the b and a files for their rooks and a single kingside pawn island. This is the mainline today. === Attack the pawn chain later === Black can focus on developing before deciding how to attack White's centre. [[/3...d6|'''3...d6''']], planning an eventual break on e6, is called the '''Hromádka system'''. The pawn on d6 controls e5, prevents e2-e4-e5 kicking Black's knight, and affording Black time to develop with ...g6, ...Bg7, and ...O-O. ...d6 also freed the d7 square for Black's queenside knight, who otherwise was relegated to developing to a6 on the side of the board. Black can start with their kingside development first instead, [[/3...g6|'''3...g6''']]. Once White plays e4, Black is compelled to play ...d6 to prevent e5! and these approaches transpose. === Play around the pawn chain === Black can choose to play around the pawn chain instead. [[/3...e5|'''3...e5?!''']], the '''Czech-Benoni''', looks to close up the centre instead. After 4. Nc3 d6 5. e4 however, White is afforded much more space and can play for pawn breaks on either flank. [[/3...Ne4|'''3...Ne4?!''']] the '''Vulture defence''', was a sideline popular in the 90s. === History === 3...e6, the Modern Benoni, was popular in the 1970s-1980s with counter-attacking players like Champions [[wikipedia:Mikhail Tal|Tal]], [[wikipedia:Bobby Fischer|Fischer]], and [[wikipedia:Garry Kasparov|Kasparov]], until the discovery of of the Taimanov variation, 4. Nc3 exd5 5.cxd5 d6 6.e4 g6 7.f4 Bg7 8.Bb5+!, rendered the Benoni all but unplayable. Thus, nowadays most players will choose a different move-order to reach the Benoni: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6, and if White plays 3. Nc3, then Black satisfies himself with 3...Bb4, the Nimzo-Indian, but if White plays the anti-Nimzo with 3. Nf3, then after 3...c5 4. d5 exd5 5.cxd5 d6 6. Nc3 g6 then f4 is no longer possible. White will have to satisfy himself with either the old main line, 7. e4 Bg7 8. Be2, the current main line, 7. h3 Bg7 8. e4 O-O 9. Bd3, or the Fianchetto Variation, 7. g3 Bg7 8. Bg2. The Benko or Volga Gambit was revived by Hungarian-American grandmaster [[wikipedia:Pal Benko|Pal Benko]] in the early 1970s after it enjoyed a brief period of popularity in the mid-1950s. However, today it is judged as +/= because Black has no tactical chances, and practice has shown that White can weather the storm, keeping his extra pawn. Alternatively, the Zaitsev line is very sharp and complicated, when White plays 5. Nc3 axb5 6. e4 b4 7. Nb5. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}}. '''1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 c5 3. d5'''

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Budapest defence |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A51-A52]] |parent=[[../|Indian Defence]] }} == 2...e5 · Budapest defence ==

Almost a respectable opening.

— [[wikipedia:Boris Avrukh|Boris Avrukh]]{{cite book | author=Avrukh, Boris | title=1.d4 Volume Two | publisher=Quality Chess | isbn=978-1-906552-33-6 | page=91 | year=2010}}
'''2...e5''' is the energetic Budapest defence, aka the Budapest gambit. Black challenges White's centre straight away. Black sacrifices a pawn, but can usually recover it, in return for active play. It's one of those slightly inaccurate sort of lines that is usually described as a "good blitz/surprise weapon". [[/3. dxe5|'''3. dxe5''']], '''accepting the gambit''', is the main line. White takes the pawn and compels Black's knight to move again, either to g4 or e4. White is up a pawn but it may be a mistake to hold onto it too tightly. Returning it allows White to avoid tactical complications (in the main line continuation, it is returned after 3...Ng4 4. Bf4 Nc6 5. Nf3 Bb4+ 6. Nbd2 Qe7, and White cannot add a further defender). '''Declining the gambit''' is atypical. Surely Black shouldn't be allowed a free potshot at White's centre? * [[/3. e3|'''3. e3?!''']] prepares to recapture the pawn, but allows Black to equalise. A continuation is 3...exd4 4. exd4 Bb4+ 5. Nc3 O-O 6. Bd3 d5{{Chess/not|}}A sample game: [https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1306553 Ravbinovich v Mieses, 1908 - Chessgames.com] 0-1 (transposition from a King's English). * [[/3. Nf3|'''3. Nf3?!''']] to defend the pawn allows 3...e5 to drive the knight away. * [[/3. d5|'''3. d5?!''']] to avoid the capture is a positional mistake, and releases the c5 square for Black's bishop. === History === The Budapest is first known from a 1896 game between amateur Mór Adler and [[Wikipedia:Géza Maróczy|Géza Maróczy]] (1870―1951) in Budapest.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1503218 Adler v Maroczy, 1896 - Chessgames.com] It was revisited in 1916, again in Budapest, by [[wikipedia:Gyula Breyer|Gyula Breyer]] (1893―1921) as Black against [[wikipedia:Jan F. Esser|Johannes Esser]] (1877―1946)[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1529568 Esser v Breyer, 1916 - Chessgames.com] and came to prominence when [[wikipedia:Milan Vidmar|Milan Vidmar]] (1885―1962) scored an upset with it against [[wikipedia:Akiba Rubinstein|Akiba Rubinstein]] (1880―1961).[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1119780 Rubinstein v Vidmar, 1918 - Chessgames.com] ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e5'''

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |Budapest defence |eco=[[Chess/ECOA|A51-A52]] |parent=[[../|Budapest defence]] }} == 3. dxe5 == White accepts the free pawn. This comes with tempo on Black's knight, so Black's must decide where to move it. [[/3...Ng4|'''3...Ng4''']] is the '''main line Budapest'''. This saves the knight and prepares to recapture the pawn. The next few moves revolve around the defence of or attack on the e5 pawn. After 4. Nf3, the Adler variation, White usually can't bring enough defenders so allows Black to take the pawn back and prioritises their piece development instead. Alekhine advocated 4. e4, giving the pawn back immediately without a fight. In the main line, 4. Bf4, the Rubinstein variation, White does have the choice of hanging onto the pawn, but only if they decide it is worth having doubled c-pawns themselves. The alternative is [[/3...Ne4|'''3...Ne4''']], the '''Fajarowicz variation'''. Black sees no urgency in recovering the pawn and would rather prioritise activity. ==Theory table== {{Chess Opening Theory/Table}} '''1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5'''

{{Chess Opening Theory/Position |name=Krejcik variation |eco=[[Chess/ECOB|B02]] |parent=[[../|Alekhine's defence]] }} == 2. Bc4? · Krejcik variation == White leaves the e4-pawn undefended. Though they can recover the pawn tactically with Bxf2+ this riposte from White is not as dangerous as it looks and Black ends up with a superior position. [[/2...Nxe4|'''2...Nxe4''']] takes the hanging pawn. To recover the material, White has a flashy manoeuvre where they sacrifice the bishop and trade for Black's knight. 3. Bxf7+ Kxf7 4. Qh5+ (4. Qf3+?? Nf6 {{Chess/not|---}}}) Kg8 5. Qd5+ e6 6. Qxe4. However, White has given up their space advantage, while Black's king is quite safe and they have easy development. 6...d5 7. Qe2 e5! (sacrificing the e-pawn to open their bishop and develop with tempo) 8. Qxe5 Nc6. Black is far ahead in development. There is therefore no reason why Black should wish to avoid taking the pawn, but alternatives include '''2...d5!?''' 3. exd5 Nxd5 (3. Bxd5? Nxd5 4. exd5 Qxd5 and watch out for Black's attack on g2). [[/2...e5|'''2...e5!?''']] transposes into the bishop's opening. === History === [[w:Josef Krejcik|Josef Krejcik]] (1885―1957) was an Austrian chess master who originated this line in 1922.[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chessgame?gid=1243030 Krejcik v Gottlieb, 1922. Chessgames.com] A poor defence by Black led to their resignation on turn seven (see sample game). == Sample game == '''Josef Krejcik v. Adolf Gottlieb, 1922.'''
'''Landstrasser Schachbund, Vienna.''' '''1. e4 Nf6 2. Bc4''' The Krejcik variation, an unconventional continuation of the Alekhine defence. '''2...d6!?''' Better was simply to take the pawn, 2...Nxe4. 3. Bxf7+ Kxf7 4. Qh5+ Kg8 5. Qd5+ e6 6. Qxe4 d5 7. Qe2 e5! Qxe5 Nc6 {{chess/not|--}}. Perhaps Black is wary of White's unusual continuation and contemplates transposing into a solid Pirc defence for safety. '''3. Nc3 Nxe4?''' Only now, having given White the opportunity to bring out another defender of the pawn, does Black take the pawn. If 4. Nxe4 d5! 5. Bd3 dxe4 6. Bxe4, material is even and Black has the initiative. '''4. Bxf7+! Kxf7 5. Nxe4''' Black loses castling rights, but the position is close to even. '''5...e5 6. Qf3+ Kg8??''' 6...Ke8 and Black is still in the game. '''7. Ng5 1-0''' Threatens 8. Qf7#. If 7...Qxg5 8. Qd5+! Be6 9. Qxe6#. The best defence is to give up a bishop: 7...Be6 8. Nxe6 Qe7. Black resigns. == Theory table == {{ChessTable}} {{Chess/theory table |line1=2. ... Nxe4 3.
